You have 1000 words.

It's a strange kind of gift, isn't it? Not money, not time, but words. A finite pile of them placed in your hands with the instruction: *spend them however you want.*

Most people, when given a limit, immediately feel it as a cage. 1000 words isn't that much. It's not a novel. It's barely a short story. It's a few pages double-spaced. You could use them to argue, to explain, to apologize. You could waste them.

So what comes to me, when told I can write whatever I want?

This: The quiet panic of a blank page.

I think about the old library on 5th Street that they tore down last year. Not because it was important, but because it wasn't. It was a small brick building squeezed between a laundromat and a bodega, the kind of place that always smelled faintly of old coffee and floor wax. I used to go there after school when I was twelve, not to read, but to be cool. The air conditioning was too strong in the summer and the heating clanked too loud in the winter, but Mrs. Albright, the librarian, never told you to leave.

Mrs. Albright had a cart she called The Island of Misfit Books. These were books that had been damaged, or returned ruined, or donated and deemed not quite good enough for the shelves. Water-warped paperbacks, children's books with crayon on every page, a repair manual for a tractor no one in the city owned. She sold them for ten cents each, but if you didn't have ten cents she would trade you for a good question.

I once asked her, "Why do you keep books no one wants?"

And she said, "Because someone wanted them once. That counts for something."

I think about that a lot now. How much of our lives is made of things that someone wanted once.

If I have 1000 words, I want to spend a few of them on quiet things that don't usually get counted.

I want to spend words on the way light falls at 4:47 p.m. in late October, when it comes in sideways and gold and makes even the dust in your apartment look intentional. On the precise sound of a grocery store automatic door opening on a rainy day, that soft *shush* that means *come in, it's dry in here.*

I want to spend words on people who have almost finished something but haven't yet. The woman on the subway with knitting half-done in her lap, the blue yarn tangled around her fingers. The kid practicing parallel parking with his father gripping the door handle. The man in the park trying to teach his dog to catch a frisbee, both of them failing with total joy.

We love stories about finishes — the graduation, the wedding, the arrival. But most of life is lived in the middle. In the draft.

So let me tell you a story from the middle.

There was a man named Ellis who collected sounds.

Not music. Not in the way you'd think. He collected small, disappearing sounds that most people didn't notice. He had a little handheld recorder from the 90s, the kind that used actual tapes. He would sit on his fire escape with it.

He had the sound of the ice cream truck turning the corner two blocks away, so faint you could convince yourself you imagined it. He had the sound of his neighbor Mrs. Chen dragging her potted plants inside before a storm, the terracotta scraping concrete. He had the sound his old radiator made right before it clanged — a sigh, almost human.

His wife, June, used to tease him about it. "What are you going to do with all those noises?" she'd ask, laughing while she folded laundry.

"I don't know," he'd say. "Keep them."

When June got sick, the apartment got quieter in a way that had nothing to do with volume. The television stayed off. The kettle didn't whistle as often. Ellis found himself recording more urgently, as if he could pin the world down with sound.

He recorded June humming while she did the crossword, even though she insisted she couldn't carry a tune. He recorded her breathing while she napped on the couch with a book splayed open on her chest. He recorded her saying his name when she couldn't find her glasses. *Ellis? Ellis, have you seen—*

He didn't listen to them right away. It felt greedy.

After she was gone, he didn't listen for a long time either. The tapes sat in a shoebox in his closet for almost a year. Then one rainy Tuesday, the same kind of gray Tuesday that makes you forget what month it is, he sat at his kitchen table and pressed play.

*Hiss. Click.*

And there she was. Not in words, but in all the little sounds between words. The way she cleared her throat before she spoke. The soft tap of her fingernails on the mug.

He cried, of course. But he also laughed, because on one tape he could hear himself in the background, very clearly, trying and failing to open a jar of pickles, muttering "come on, come on" while June giggled.

He had kept what mattered without even knowing he was keeping it.

We think we need to say the big things. I love you. I forgive you. I'm proud of you. And we do. But the big things are held up by a thousand tiny sounds, a thousand tiny words that feel too small to record.

If you have ever loved someone, you know their small sounds. The way they say "anyway" when they're changing the subject. The little snort they do before they laugh for real.

That's what I want to do with my 1000 words. Not build a monument, but make a shoebox. A place to keep small things.

Because here's the secret no one tells you when you're learning to write: you will never have enough words. Not 1000, not 100,000. There will always be something left unsaid. You will always leave out the exact shade of your mother's kitchen in 1998, or the precise joke that made your best friend laugh until soda came out his nose. Language is a net, and the world is water. You will always lose something through the holes.

But that doesn't mean you shouldn't cast it.

So if you're reading this, with your own finite pile of time and attention — which is even rarer than words — let me trade you. Just like Mrs. Albright and her ten-cent books.

I'll ask you a question, if you'll sit with it for a moment after you're done.

What small sound would you keep, if you could keep only one?

Would it be someone calling your name from another room? Would it be the thump of your dog jumping off the bed in the morning? Would it be the city bus sighing to a stop, doors opening with that hydraulic wheeze that means you're almost home?

Don't answer right away. Wait until the room is quiet. Wait until you hear the refrigerator hum, or the traffic outside, or your own breathing.

That sound. That's the one. Keep it.

You have — I have — we have so few words, really. But we can spend them trying to point at what can't be said. We can spend them trying to say: *I was here. You were here. This mattered.*

I started with 1000 words. I'm down to my last few now. I can feel them thinning out.

So I'll leave you with this: If you have words left today, don't save them. Spend them. Text someone something small and true. Write down one ordinary thing you saw. Say out loud a name you miss.

Use the words before they run out.
